blocks.x: STAT 153 · Statistical Methods · Topic 2

Before any mean, median or standard deviation can be calculated, data must first be found, gathered and organised correctly. This topic covers where data comes from, how it is collected, how a questionnaire is built, the full sequence of a statistical investigation, and the ethical duties every researcher carries.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Data Data in probability and statistics are the recorded observations or measurements obtained from individuals, objects, or events during a study or experiment. In simple terms, data are the basic raw material needed for any statistical work.

Primary data Primary data are original data that have been observed or collected directly from firsthand experience. They are obtained from the subjects of interest, and must be actively collected by the researcher.
Secondary data Secondary data are already compiled data — information that already exists and is readily available, rather than having to be freshly collected.
Sources of Data→ Collection Methods→ Questionnaire Design→ Stages of Investigation→ Ethics
Where the numbers come from

We often see data already neat and collated in a database, but every dataset started somewhere. The data needed for a statistical investigation are either readily available or must be collected — these are the two basic sources of data.
Primary vs. secondary data
Primary data Original data that have been observed or collected directly from firsthand experience, obtained from the subjects of interest themselves. Data that must be collected.
Secondary data Already compiled data. Data that are already available, usually gathered by someone else for a different original purpose, and then reused.
Sources of primary and secondary data in the medical field
Advantages of primary and secondary data
Primary data

items: Specific to the research purpose
Accurate and reliable (controlled by researcher)
Up-to-date, reflects current conditions
Flexible design (surveys, experiments, observations)
Authentic, firsthand information
Control over quality and sampling

blocks.x: Secondary data

items: Cost-effective and inexpensive
Time-saving, readily available
Large scope, covers wide populations
Useful for trend and historical analysis
Provides background and context
Broad coverage across regions and topics

blocks.x: Quick comparison: primary vs. secondary data

items: A researcher hands out a fresh questionnaire to patients in a clinic → primary data — collected firsthand for this specific study.
A researcher pulls patient records from an existing Electronic Health Record system → secondary data — already compiled by someone else, for another purpose.
A team designs and runs a new clinical trial → primary data — original data generated by the researcher's own experiment.
A team consults WHO global health statistics to study disease trends → secondary data — already available, international, historical.

blocks.x: Turning a plan into numbers

Planning for data collection before it actually happens is essential. No single method can fully measure the variable of interest — the statistician decides which method is best for that particular investigation.
Five planning questions
Having appropriate answers to these questions before data collection begins can yield desirable results:

items: 1How is the data collected?
2When is the data collected?
3Who is responsible for collecting and recording data?
4Where is the collected data stored?
5How do we ensure the data is correct?

blocks.x: Four main data collection methods

1. Interviews
Data collected through direct, spoken interaction between a data collector and a respondent, allowing questions to be clarified and follow-up probing on the spot.

2. Self-Administered Questionnaire
A structured research tool sent to respondents, who read, understand and answer the questions on their own, without a researcher present to guide them. (Covered in full detail in the next tab.)

3. Biometric & Physiological Measurements
Data gathered by directly measuring physical or physiological characteristics of subjects (e.g. blood pressure, height, weight, biometric readings) rather than by asking them questions.

4. Observation and Experimentation
Data collected by watching and recording behaviour or events as they occur (observation), or by deliberately manipulating conditions and recording the outcome (experimentation).

Each method carries its own advantages and disadvantages, and there are a number of other methods beyond these four. No one method can fully capture the variable of interest on its own — the choice of method is a judgement call made by the statistician for that particular investigation.

blocks.title: Why does planning matter before collecting data?

items: Deciding how and when data is collected in advance avoids inconsistent or incomparable measurements later.
Knowing who is responsible for collection and recording keeps accountability clear and reduces missing or duplicated data.
Deciding where data will be stored protects it from loss and keeps it organised for later analysis.
Building in a check for correctness from the outset catches errors early, rather than after the investigation is complete.

blocks.x: Asking the right questions, the right way

A questionnaire is one of the most widely used data collection tools — but a poorly made one can create practical difficulties during the survey and lead to wrong conclusions when results are analysed. Careful design is essential.
What is a questionnaire?

Questionnaire A structured research tool made up of a series of questions designed to collect information from people about their opinions, behaviours, experiences, or characteristics. It is mailed or sent to respondents, who are expected to read and understand the questions and write down the reply in the space provided — respondents answer the questions on their own.
There are three types of questionnaire:

items: SStructured — a fixed set of questions asked in a fixed order, usually with predefined response options.
SSSemi-structured — a mix of fixed questions and open-ended questions, allowing some flexibility in responses.
UUnstructured — open-ended, with no fixed wording or order, allowing the respondent to answer freely in their own words.

blocks.x: Three steps in designing a questionnaire

1. Designing the Instrument
• A questionnaire should remain short.
• The questions must be clear, simple, and easy to understand.
• The question must avoid testing memory, being personal, offensive, or leading.
• The instrument should be organized in a logical sequence.

2. Pretesting in Pilot Survey
• Testing a questionnaire with a small group before the main survey is very important.
• Pilot testing ensures the questions are clear and provides early data for study design.

3. Editing Results
• Completed questionnaires are reviewed and edited to minimize errors.
• Computer tools now help spot outliers (unusual responses), which often result from mistakes or false information.
Advantages and disadvantages of the questionnaire method
Advantages

items: Cost-effective
Free from bias of the interviewer
Respondents who are not easily approachable can still be reached conveniently
Scalability — large samples can be reached quickly, making results more reliable
Standardization — all respondents receive the same questions, ensuring consistency in data collection
Anonymity — encourages honest answers, especially on sensitive topics

blocks.x: Disadvantages

items: Can be used only when respondents are educated and cooperating
Control of the questionnaire may be lost once it is sent
Low response rates
Misinterpretation — respondents may misunderstand questions without clarification
Technical barriers — online surveys exclude those without internet access

blocks.x: Advantages and disadvantages by aspect

c: Low cost, efficient for large samples
May still require resources for design/admin

blocks.title: Why do the three design steps matter, in order?

items: Designing the instrument first, with short, clear, unbiased and logically sequenced questions, gives the pilot survey something sound to test.

Pretesting in a pilot survey catches confusing or badly worded questions before they are sent out to the full sample — a mistake caught here is cheap; the same mistake caught after the main survey is expensive.
Editing results happens last, once real responses exist, and uses tools (including computer-assisted outlier detection) to catch mistakes or false information in what was actually returned.

sections.title: The 9 stages of a statistical investigation

blocks.x: From problem to published result

If an investigation is to optimize the use of available resources, expertise, and time, it is essential to carefully examine all aspects of the design and application of statistical investigations — experiments and surveys — at the planning level, from problem statement through to final report.

9stages, from statement of the problem to interpretation and presentation of results 3categories of required resources: physical, human, financial 6core ethical considerations every researcher must follow
The 9 stages of a statistical investigation

1. Statement of Problems and Objectives An investigation must have a clearly defined and precise objective to guide data collection and analysis. Key points: • Identify the cause for concern and state the problem explicitly. • Translate the objective into definitions of characteristics to be measured, and specifications for collecting, processing, and publishing data. • Ensure the objective is clear, precise, and unambiguous. • A well-stated objective provides a reference framework for collecting relevant data.

2. Target Population and the Use of Sample or Entire Population Clearly define the population of interest; sampling depends on unit definition and design choice. Key points: • Define the population clearly and unambiguously. • Sampling units should be distinct, current, non-overlapping, and cover the entire population. • Units must be locatable — important for mobile populations. • Sampling design depends on variability, cost, and time. • Expert input is often required.

3. Design of Questionnaire or Schedule
• Questionnaire construction is extremely important because respondents and data collectors must interpret the questions.
• It requires skill, special techniques, and familiarity with the subject matter.
• Use expert-designed and pre-tested questions whenever possible.

4. Method of Data Collection and Fieldwork
• Choose an appropriate data collection method (interview, telephone, mail, observation, or existing sources) based on cost and accuracy.
• Train personnel thoroughly in locating sample units, recording measurements, and applying collection methods.
• Success of the investigation depends on reliable fieldwork.
• Provide adequate supervisory staff for inspection and quality control after fieldwork.

5. Required Data
The data to be collected should be guided by the objective of the investigation.

6. List of Available Resources Investigations require physical, human, and financial resources to ensure effective data collection and analysis. Key points: • Physical: sampling frame, field manuals, computer facilities. • Human: survey experts, data collectors, analysts. • Financial: funds for planning, analysis, and computer time.
7. Conducting a Pilot Survey A pilot survey (also known as pre-testing) is a survey carried out before the main one. It is conducted to test the techniques of the survey, not to collect viable data.

8. Data Handling
Collection, editing, storage, and organization of data.

9. Interpretation and Presentation of Results
The final stage of a survey involves preparing a simple report that presents the design, terms of reference, and findings with tables and charts, interprets results clearly, and offers recommendations with future directions.
Problem & Objectives→ Population & Sample→ Questionnaire Design→ Collection Method & Fieldwork→ Required Data→ Available Resources→ Pilot Survey→ Data Handling→ Interpretation & Presentation
Ethical considerations for data collection

Every profession is guided by a code of ethics that reflects evolving values, needs, and stakeholder expectations. This ethical framework also governs how research is conducted, placing responsibility on individuals to adhere to the following codes in their professional practice.

items: 1Seek Consent — obtain informed agreement from participants before collecting their data.
2Avoid Bias — design and conduct the investigation so that results are not skewed by the researcher's own preferences or assumptions.
3Maintain confidentiality and respect for privacy — protect respondents' identities and personal information.
4Use appropriate research methodology — choose methods suited to the investigation's objectives and population.
5Avoid use of data for discriminatory or unethical purposes — never use collected data to disadvantage or harm groups of people.
6Use appropriate language for respondents — communicate in a way respondents can understand, respecting their background and literacy.

blocks.title: Quick self-check: which stage or ethical principle applies?

items: A team writes down exactly what problem they are investigating and what characteristics they will measure → Stage 1: Statement of Problems and Objectives.
A team runs a small trial survey purely to check whether their questions work, without treating the results as real data → Stage 7: Conducting a Pilot Survey.
A team budgets for data collectors' salaries and analysis software → Stage 6: List of Available Resources (financial and human).
A researcher asks a patient to sign an agreement before enrolling them in a survey → Seek Consent.
A researcher keeps patient names and identifying details locked away from published results → Maintain confidentiality and respect for privacy.
